title: Two Trains, One Fly
prompt: Two trains start 100 miles apart and travel toward each other, each at 50 miles per hour.

At the moment they begin moving, a fly sitting on the front of train A takes off and flies toward train B at 75 miles per hour. When it reaches train B, it immediately turns around and flies back toward train A — and continues bouncing back and forth until the trains collide.
How many miles does the fly travel in total?
hints: The hard way: sum an infinite series of shorter and shorter fly trips. There is a much easier approach.
Focus not on the fly's path but on the time available. How long until the trains meet?
Distance = speed × time. You know the fly's speed and the total time it flies.
solution_lede:
The trap is trying to calculate the fly's infinite back-and-forth legs and sum them up. When John von Neumann was posed this problem, he gave the answer instantly — then admitted, to laughter, that he had summed the infinite series rather than spotting the shortcut.

The elegant approach: ignore the fly's path entirely and focus on time. The two trains are 100 miles apart and closing at a combined speed of 100 mph (50 + 50). They meet in exactly 1 hour.

The fly is in the air for that entire 1 hour, travelling at 75 mph. Distance = 75 × 1 = 75 miles.

solution_steps.body: The trains close at 50 + 50 = 100 mph. Starting 100 miles apart, they meet after 1 hour.
The fly flies continuously for exactly 1 hour at 75 mph.
